query: For high-entropy alloys used in thermal-insulation applications, what testable hypothesis could be made about an unspecified predictive approach for accurately identifying materials with low phonon thermal conductivity? The hypothesis should explain why the approach would work, predict its improvement over current predictions, define its applicability limits, identify supporting evidence, and specify a decisive experimental benchmark and outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A predictive approach that explicitly incorporates measures of local chemical fluctuations (e.g., quantified force-constant variations due to severe lattice distortion) will more accurately identify high-entropy alloys with low lattice thermal conductivity compared to traditional prediction models. This is because the approach captures key mediators of phonon scattering specific to multi‐element disordered systems.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase, solid-solution high-entropy alloys (e.g., FeCoCrMnNi-type or similar systems) exhibiting severe lattice distortion and moderate force-constant fluctuations (~20–50%) relevant for thermal-insulation applications.
generation.intervention: Application of the novel predictive approach that transforms raw compositional features into expandable descriptors capturing local chemical fluctuation effects on phonon scattering, used to screen candidate HEAs.
generation.conditions: Tests performed at room temperature and at elevated temperatures typical of thermal-insulation applications, ensuring the alloys are in the single-phase, chemically disordered state.
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical fluctuations and the resultant force-constant distortions that modulate acoustic phonon attenuation and, consequently, lattice thermal conductivity.
generation.mechanism: The approach leverages the established correlation between severe lattice distortions (induced by multi-element mixing) and enhanced phonon scattering. By quantitatively incorporating descriptors related to chemical fluctuation, the model more accurately predicts when the alloy’s structure will yield phonon transport suppression, leading to a low thermal conductivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The predictive model is expected to improve the accuracy of identifying HEAs with lattice thermal conductivity in the low range (e.g., near or below 1 W/m·K) by at least 10–20% compared to conventional techniques that do not include detailed disorder descriptors.
generation.baseline: Current prediction methods, which are typically based on traditional ab initio or machine learning models trained on simpler binary/ternary systems, generally offer less accurate predictions in the context of the complex chemical disorder seen in HEAs.
generation.boundary: This approach is applicable to single-phase, chemically disordered high-entropy alloys where local force-constant fluctuations are significant. It may not perform well for alloys that are weakly disordered, multi-phase, or have extreme segregation not captured by the descriptors.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the improvement over conventional models and the universality of the approach across all HEA compositions remain uncertain until further systematic experimental validation is completed.

falsification_experiment.design: Screen a set of candidate HEAs using the predictive approach to select alloys expected to have low lattice thermal conductivity (<1 W/m·K). Synthesize the selected alloys and characterize their phonon dispersion relations using neutron scattering or inelastic X-ray scattering, complemented by GVDOS measurements. Compare the experimentally measured κL values and phonon attenuation features with the model predictions.
measurements: Lattice thermal conductivity (κL) at multiple temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the predictive approach does not yield a statistically significant improvement (e.g., prediction error reduced by at least 10–20% relative to traditional models) or if the measured lattice thermal conductivities of the synthesized HEAs are consistently and significantly higher (e.g., >20% deviation) than the predicted values, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This work shed light on the effect of constituent elements on local chemical fluctuation and lattice thermal conductivity in high-entropy thermoelectric materials and also revealed the direct relationship between the fluctuation and atomic characteristic of elements, which could serve as a guide for tailoring local chemical fluctuation in the community of high-entropy materials.

Recently, entropy engineering has been used as a novel strategy to optimize the electrical and thermal transport properties of TE materials. By increasing element species, the mixing entropy in a material system increases quickly, and high-entropy materials with over five principal elements will be formed. Severe lattice distortion is usually the core phenomenon of high-entropy material—such distortion leads to strong scattering for heat-carrying phonons and results in low lattice thermal conductivity. Stabilizing single-phase structures by increasing entropy weakens the phase-boundary electron scattering in multiphase high-entropy material, thus providing a beneficial contribution to improve electrical transport properties, i.e., entropy-driven structural stabilization,. Therefore, the high-entropy-stabilized composition should work as a good matrix for further optimization of TE performance by integrating the traditional optimization strategy.

In conclusion, we have reported the first experimental investigation of the acoustic phonon dispersions in a High-Entropy Alloy, complemented by the GVDOS survey, at room and low temperature. FeCoCrMnNi is a 5-element random alloy, and, despite the inherent disorder, its phonon dynamics closely resemble that of the pure elements composing it and the corresponding binary alloys. More specifically, acoustic phonons disperse throughout the whole Brillouin zone up to energies between 20 and 30 meV, exhibiting an attenuation stronger than in simple elements, but of the same order of magnitude as in binary alloys. The whole attenuation behavior can be understood in terms of scattering from force-constant fluctuations, which have been estimated to amount to ~20% using a simple theoretical model, a value comparable with calculations of Mu and co-authors on binary and ternary alloys made of the same elements. cited_evidence.text: Using the same approach, the value of κL was computed for various temperatures in the range 300–700 K (Figure 9). At 300 K, the κL value is 0.4 W K−1 m−1, which is a very low value of the lattice thermal conductivity, favorable for thermoelectric materials. This is due to the lattice distortion effect of high-entropy alloys that can reduce phonon velocity and enhance phonon scattering, resulting in low thermal conductivity. Additionally, one can observe that when the temperature rises, the thermal conductivity of the lattice decreases, which is also due to an increase in phonon scattering at higher temperatures.
